precepts.text: And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David. So we know who this is speaking of.
precepts.point: You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just did not care, and he went the extra mile: later in the story he put Uriah in the front of the battle and got him killed, then took the wife. What he saw became desire, desire became action, he tried to cover it up, and the consequences came: the child died.

note.label: Satan's Kiss To Your Demise

precepts.why:
“And after him rose up Nathan to prophesy in the time of David.” So we know who we are talking about: this is David, in the days of Nathan the prophet, the prophet the Lord sent to him after Bathsheba. The next verse carries on: “As is the fat taken away from the peace offering, so was David chosen out of the children of Israel.”

That is the same David of 2 Samuel 11. He went out on the roof, “he saw a woman washing herself; and the woman was very beautiful to look upon.” Bad to the bone. He sent and inquired: I got power, let me send some people over there, let me make this official. One with a spiritual mind made it plain: this is the wife of Uriah the Hittite, this is somebody's wife, bro. “And David sent messengers, and took her” anyway. Wisdom and understanding were right there, and he pushed them aside.

“and she came in unto him, and he lay with her”. She wasn't right either. She didn't resist, she wasn't opposed; she thought she came up. “And the woman conceived, and sent and told David, and said, I am with child.”

You see how Satan can deceive you. Satan put that lust in him to where he just didn't care, and he went the extra mile: he put Uriah in the front of the battle, got him killed, and took the wife. What he saw, the desire, the action, the cover-up, and the consequences: his first child was gone. Yet Sirach remembers David as the one chosen out of the children of Israel, and that leads to what the Lord did with him.

precepts.text: The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel. The Lord forgave David; he loved David, and David messed up badly. A lot of times we are going to fall and do things that are not comely according to the scriptures. That does not mean you bunker down into a fetal position and say woe is me. You get yourself together, you repent, and you move forward. What did Christ say? Go, and sin no more. You pick up the pieces and keep moving. We are all going to make mistakes; it is how you handle the mistake.

precepts.why:
“The Lord took away his sins, and exalted his horn for ever: he gave him a covenant of kings, and a throne of glory in Israel.” The Lord did forgive David. He loved David, and David messed up.

David saw Bathsheba from the roof, took another man's wife, put Uriah in battle to be killed, and lost the child. That is as bad as it gets. But David repented, and the Lord took away his sins, exalted his horn, and gave him a covenant of kings and a throne of glory in Israel.

And that's another thing. A lot of times we are going to fall and do things that are not comely according to the scriptures. That don't mean you bunker down, go into a fetal position and say woe is me. You get yourself together, you repent, and you move forward. You don't go back. What did Christ say? Go, and sin no more.

You got to pick up the pieces and keep moving. We are all going to make mistakes. It is how you handle the mistake: it happened, so what are you going to do now, moving forward?

precepts.text: In all Israel there was none so much praised as Absalom for his beauty, without blemish from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. Beauty became his identity, and behind it came ambition, rebellion against his father, civil war, and death hanging by that very hair. Whenever physical attraction is in the forefront, the Bible shows trouble behind it.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“But in all Israel there was none to be so much praised as Absalom for his beauty: from the sole of his foot even to the crown of his head there was no blemish in him.” Beauty became part of Absalom's identity. It was synonymous with him: his hair, his physical perfection.

And what came behind that? Ambition and rebellion. You get a big head about yourself and you start to believe certain things. Absalom rose up against his father, it came to civil war, and he died hanging from that very hair, the same thing that was vanity to him.

That is the same lesson as David on the roof in 2 Samuel 11:2. David saw a woman “very beautiful to look upon”, he saw her, he inquired, and he took her, the same pattern as Shechem with Dinah. Out of one fleeting moment of attraction came adultery, the murder of Uriah, a national scandal, the death of the child, and chaos in David's house the rest of his days. The Lord forgave him, but he left him with drama for moving that way. Then Absalom, celebrated for his own beauty, came to pride and rebellion.

Whenever physical attraction becomes the forefront of anything, the Bible shows you that trouble comes behind it. Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage: she look good, I got to marry her so I can have her. Attraction is the gateway to destruction if that is the only thing you are moving on.

precepts.text: Lust not after her beauty in thine heart, neither let her take thee with her eyelids. She gives you the look back, the sparks fly, and you have lost your mind.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
This is why the scripture says these things: “Lust not after her beauty in thine heart; neither let her take thee with her eyelids.” The scripture teaches you not to lust after her beauty, and it says where: in thy heart, in thy mind.

“neither let her take thee with her eyelids.” She gives you the look back. You make the eye contact, you feel the chemistry, the sparks fly, the tentacles of auras come out and they embrace, and you done lost your mind. I got to have her. Bring me that. That's what I want.

That is exactly what happened to David in 2 Samuel 11:2. He walked on the roof, saw a woman washing herself, “and the woman was very beautiful to look upon”, and he moved on what he saw. Shechem saw Dinah and took her, and it ended in violence and massacre. Samson went after the one who pleased him well, and it ended in betrayal and blindness. David saw Bathsheba's beauty, had to have her, and it ended in adultery and murder.

So Solomon's warning is the guard against the very thing David fell into: do not let the beauty get into your heart, and do not let the eyes take you. Attraction is not the foundation, and a man who moves on it alone gives up his strength.

precepts.text: A woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart. The physical again, meant to entice, and it works. Solomon knew how intoxicating it is; he said not one woman in a thousand.
precepts.point: Y'all take chess and spades seriously, seeing moves ahead and counting books, but not marriage. She looks good, I have to marry her so I can have her.

note.label: Marriage Beyond Romance: From Eden to Modern Confusion

precepts.why:
“And, behold, there met him a woman with the attire of an harlot, and subtil of heart.” There is the physical again: the attire of an harlot and subtil of heart. She is trying to entice, and you fall for it. It works.

Here Solomon warns about being captured by appearance. How does he know these things? He said not one out of a thousand of the women he dealt with. He knew, and he probably knew before the thousandth. It goes to show how intoxicating it can be. You get caught up.

That is the thread through David on the roof in 2 Samuel 11:2. Shechem saw Dinah and took her: violence and massacre. Samson, she pleased him well: betrayal and blindness. David saw Bathsheba's beauty and had to have her: adultery and murder. Absalom, celebrated for his own beauty: pride and rebellion. And the strange women, being beautiful, lead to ruin.

That is why the Bible rarely makes much of the beauty of wives. Rebecca is known for her character, her hospitality and her faith; Zipporah's beauty is never described; Elizabeth is called righteous, not beautiful. What is highlighted in our foremothers is righteousness, obedience, wisdom and faith. The Bible doesn't deny attraction; it just isn't the foundation.

precepts.text: Cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.
precepts.point: David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

precepts.why:
“Cursed be he that smiteth his neighbour secretly. And all the people shall say, Amen. Cursed be he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person.”

David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah himself: “Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.” Joab assigned him to a place where he knew valiant men were, “and Uriah the Hittite died also.”

David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. He smote his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing. And he took reward to slay an innocent person: the reward was that woman, and he slew an innocent man who had done nothing. Both curses fall on this deed.

precepts.text: Joab was David's nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah; Joab knew David's dirt, which is why he often defied the king's orders.
precepts.point: Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder; he could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bore Joab's armor compassed Absalom and smote him and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

note.label: 2 Samuel 18: Deal Gently With the Young Man

precepts.why:
At “the time when kings go forth to battle”, David sent Joab out against the children of Ammon, “But David tarried still at Jerusalem.” From the roof he saw Bath-sheba, sent and took her, and when she was with child, “David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.”

Joab was David’s nephew and the go between in the matter of Bathsheba and the killing of Uriah. Joab knew David’s dirt, which is why he often defied the king’s orders.

And here he defied them. The man who saw Absalom hanged in an oak would not touch him for a thousand shekels, “for in our hearing the king charged thee and Abishai and Ittai, saying, Beware that none touch the young man Absalom.” Joab said, “I may not tarry thus with thee”, took three darts, “and thrust them through the heart of Absalom, while he was yet alive in the midst of the oak.”

Joab was an evil man with the spirit of murder. He could have brought Absalom back alive for his father to make amends, but he did what he wanted. Ten young men that bare Joab’s armour compassed about and smote Absalom and slew him, for a beast will consort to his own like.

points: And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die. Somebody explain what just happened. From the floor: King David just plotted against Uriah, for Bathsheba, to set him up to be killed in the battle.

But hold on a second. Did King Saul not try to do that to him? Same thing. Remember I made a statement earlier that you may not be tempted by that bitterness now. Just wait. So right now King David is no longer on the run. He is back in his kingship, back in his palace, back in his rightful place. And that same spirit tempted him. And his was through coveting his neighbour's house. So through that covetousness it compounded with hatred and bitterness.

So a lot of the time we are like, oh no, I am not dealing with that. Do you think David thought, when he was running from King Saul, that he would have to be dealing with the same thing? Everyone always thinks all Bishop's classes are about everybody else. All the deacon's classes are about everybody else. Well, which one is about you? Just give it time.

points: After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child.

Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city.

note.label: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah

points: When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High.

It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.
